title: Rethinking Prediction Horizons: Decoupling Model Queries from State Updates in Few-Step MeanFlow

paper.title: Rethinking Prediction Horizons: Decoupling Model Queries from State Updates in Few-Step MeanFlow
paper.abstract: Abstract MeanFlow predicts interval-average velocities, but conventional few-step sampling ties the interval queried from the model to the duration of the state update. We separate these two quantities at inference, fixing the model, update grid, and number of queries while varying the prediction horizon. Our central finding is that the horizon response depends on both query position and the states entering that query. Across seven independently trained CIFAR-10 checkpoints at classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale 2, a longer horizon worsens FID at early steps but improves it at the midpoint. To probe whether query time alone determines this response, we fix the midpoint query and current/subsequent guidance while changing only earlier CFG. In held-out factorial outcomes on five previously studied checkpoints, the mean midpoint horizon benefit increases from 0.109 to 1.308 FID, indicating sensitivity to the incoming-state distribution. A frozen four-query rule reduces mean CIFAR-10 FID by 2.023 without retraining or extra queries, including gains on five checkpoints trained after rule selection. A milder rule also improves mean FID by 1.041 on a stronger frozen grid, with fixed-rule FID gains on the evaluated public ImageNet-256 and AFHQ checkpoints. However, matched-budget calibration favors query-start shifting in historical CIFAR tests, and the tested Horizon allocation adds no FID benefit beyond Grid+Start on two public ImageNet models. Thus, prediction horizon is a distinct, position- and state-sensitive inference control, but not a universally preferred one.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2025 ) predicts an average velocity over an interval and conventionally uses the same interval to advance the state. This couples two decisions: how far the model predicts and how far the sampler moves. Matching them gives the intended displacement for an exact interval-average predictor; a learned predictor’s approximation also depends on the requested interval. Varying prediction horizon independently of update duration exposes an inference choice hidden by their coupling. Let h k h_{k} denote the prediction horizon and δ k = t k + 1 − t k \delta_{k}=t_{k+1}-t_{k} the update duration. We study x k + 1 = x k + δ k ​ u θ ​ ( x k , t k , h k ) , x_{k+1}=x_{k}+\delta_{k}u_{\theta}(x_{k},t_{k},h_{k}), (1) with the model, query start, state grid and query count fixed. Standard inference sets h k = δ k h_{k}=\delta_{k} ; varying only h k h_{k} changes the prediction interval while preserving update duration. Earlier two-time denoisers already separate prediction intervals from output coefficients ( Lee et al., 2026a ; Zilberstein et al., 2026 ) . Our contribution is a controlled characterization of what this choice does in pretrained few-step MeanFlow. Figure 1: Horizon response reverses with position and changes with earlier guidance. Left: seven CIFAR checkpoints at CFG 2, with pointwise 95% Student- t t intervals across checkpoints. Right: five checkpoints with held-out factorial outcomes compare midpoint h 2 = .50 h_{2}=.50 versus .25 .25 after prefix CFG 1 or 1.5; current/later CFG stays 1.5. Lines connect the same checkpoint. Both panels use paired 10k samples per cell, but different guidance settings and checkpoint subsets. The main empirical result is a position-dependent sign reversal in the effect of the queried horizon (Figure 1a). With the checkpoint, state grid, update durations, and guidance fixed, extending a single horizon from 0.25 0.25 to 0.50 0.50 worsens endpoint FID at the source ( t = 0 t=0 ), but improves it at the midpoint ( t = 0.50 t=0.50 ) on all seven independently trained CIFAR checkpoints at CFG 2. A longer prediction horizon is therefore not uniformly beneficial, even at the same extension ratio h / δ = 2 h/\delta=2 . This reversal exposes behavior that cannot be captured by a global horizon multiplier. Crucially, query position alone is insufficient to characterize the horizon response (Figure 1b). We hold the midpoint query time, physical grid, and current/subsequent guidance fixed while changing only CFG in the preceding updates. Within each prefix condition, the two horizon choices share the same incoming states; across prefix conditions, earlier guidance changes the distribution of states reaching the midpoint. In held-out factorial outcomes on five previously studied checkpoints, with the hypothesis frozen before outcome inspection, the mean benefit of midpoint horizon extension increases from 0.109 0.109 to 1.308 1.308 FID. This interaction establishes sensitivity to the incoming-state distribution beyond the query time alone, although it does not isolate the contributions of CFG construction bias, prediction error, or other state-dependent effects. These observations also have practical consequences at fixed inference cost. A frozen four-query horizon rule reduces mean CIFAR-10 FID by 2.023 2.023 across seven checkpoints, including five trained after rule selection. A milder fixed rule retains a mean gain of 1.041 1.041 on a stronger frozen grid, and fixed-rule FID gains extend to the evaluated public ImageNet and AFHQ checkpoints. However, the usefulness of horizon calibration depends on the alternatives: query-start shifts can achieve lower FID/KID, and the tested Horizon allocation provides no additional FID benefit beyond Grid+Start on two public ImageNet models. We therefore distinguish the reproducible response to prediction horizon from whether allocating calibration budget to this control is optimal for a given configuration and evaluator. Our contributions are: • Position-dependent horizon response. We identify a reproducible sign reversal in the effect of extending the queried prediction horizon while preserving the physical state-update grid and model-query count. • Incoming-state dependence. Through a preceding-guidance intervention with the midpoint query and subsequent guidance fixed, we show that the horizon benefit changes with the states entering the query, rather than being determined by query time alone. • Reproducibility and competing controls. We validate frozen horizon rules across training seeds and a stronger state grid, assess fixed-rule transfer to public checkpoints, and compare horizon, query-start, and grid controls under explicit calibration budgets, identifying both benefits and limitations.

sections.heading: 3 Reproducible Gains at Fixed Query Cost
sections.text: We first test frozen horizon rules across training seeds, on a stronger fixed grid and on other evaluated models.

sections.heading: 3.1 Evaluation setup
sections.text: We evaluate class-conditional CIFAR-10, public ImageNet-256 MeanFlow-family checkpoints, and latent AFHQv2 models producing 256 × 256 256\times 256 images ( Choi et al., 2020 ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) , using FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , KID where available ( Bińkowski et al., 2018 ) , and specified supplementary evaluators. NFE counts velocity queries; two-pass CFG uses two backbone calls per query. Primary CIFAR tests use CFG 2, while temporal calibration uses CFG 1.5 under separate sample/reference protocols. The primary replication unit is an independently trained checkpoint. We evaluate seven CIFAR checkpoints from one training recipe, including five trained after the horizon rule was frozen. Generation repeats are averaged within checkpoint before equal checkpoint weighting. Public ImageNet and AFHQ checkpoints separately assess fixed-rule transfer; Section 5.3 adds two new CIFAR seeds for calibration tests. Training definitions, checkpoint provenance and repeat accounting are in Appendices A.2 and A.3 .

sections.heading: 4 Position Reversal and an Incoming-State Control
sections.text: We now vary query position and use an incoming-state control to test whether time alone determines the response.

sections.heading: What the intervention identifies.
sections.text: The benefit of the midpoint intervention depends on the distribution of states reaching that query, beyond its time coordinate alone. Because earlier guidance changes those states and FID is nonlinear, the interaction does not distinguish CFG construction bias, horizon-dependent prediction error and other state-dependent effects. Its direction is also inconsistent across the ImageNet repeats (Appendix G.2 ).

sections.heading: Why the horizon matters.
sections.text: An exact interval-average predictor favors h = δ h=\delta because the resulting update gives the intended flow displacement. Equation 5 shows what changes for a learned model: varying h h changes both the mismatch between requested and physical intervals and the predictor’s approximation error. The horizon therefore selects how the learned field is queried, in addition to the state grid’s choice of integration steps. The position reversal and incoming-state control reveal structure in this combined response. They leave the relative roles of approximation error and CFG construction bias unresolved; exploratory directional and local-reference studies examine these possibilities in Appendices E.3 and G.3 . The decomposition also clarifies why local prediction accuracy and endpoint performance need separate evaluation. Its two terms are vectors: changing their magnitudes alone does not determine the magnitude of their sum. An endpoint metric additionally evaluates the distribution after the remaining updates, which act on the states produced by the intervention. Agreement with a local reference and improvement of the final distribution therefore answer different questions. In our reference diagnostic, longer midpoint horizons move farther from both the native-local and instantaneous-Heun reference velocities even where endpoint FID improves (Appendix G.3 ). These references are constructed from the learned model, not ground-truth transport trajectories. Their disagreement with FID cautions against using local agreement as a selection criterion on its own; it does not identify the error responsible for the endpoint gain.

sections.heading: Selecting the horizon.
sections.text: Once chosen, Horizon adds no velocity queries, but the tested selectors require target rollouts. The preferred temporal control changes across models, NFE values and evaluators, and the tested diagnostic predictor fails its prespecified success criterion (Appendix G.1 ). Practical selection therefore remains target-dependent. More broadly, our experiments separate two questions: whether a model input changes endpoint behavior, and whether allocating calibration budget to that input improves on available alternatives. The position and incoming-state controls establish the former for prediction horizon; the matched-budget comparisons show that the latter is configuration dependent.

sections.heading: Scope of the finding.
sections.text: The position reversal and prospective replication are established within one guided CIFAR architecture and training recipe. The blind study adds two training seeds at NFE values already seen in development. Fixed-rule FID gains transfer to the listed public checkpoints, but native iMF interventions fail their benefit criterion (Appendix G.2 ). Together with the Start comparisons and metric trade-offs, this evidence supports configuration-specific horizon calibration. A transferable rule for choosing the horizon remains a separate research challenge.

sections.heading: Few-step MeanFlow inference.
sections.text: MeanFlow predicts interval-average velocities ( Geng et al., 2025 ) ; subsequent work studies training stability, guidance and gap curricula ( Geng et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . MeanCache constructs interval averages through Jacobian–vector-product reuse ( Gao et al., 2026 ) . Decoupled MeanFlow reassigns time conditioning across backbone blocks, studies conversion with and without fine-tuning, and uses restart/CTM samplers that can request an intermediate endpoint before a separate state transition ( Lee et al., 2026b ) . Our deterministic intervention retains the existing model interface, query start and physical grid.

sections.heading: Two-time denoisers and prediction horizon.
sections.text: Lee et al. (2026a) introduce a two-time denoiser for language modeling. Flow Map Denoisers ( Zilberstein et al., 2026 ) use D s , t ​ ( x ) = x + ( 1 − s ) ​ v ​ ( x , s , t ) D_{s,t}(x)=x+(1-s)v(x,s,t) , with v v averaged over [ s , t ] [s,t] , and vary t t to control the distortion–perception trade-off. This is an algebraic instance of Equation 1 with δ = 1 − s \delta=1-s and h = t − s ≤ δ h=t-s\leq\delta . Our empirical focus is intermediate-step generation with h > δ h>\delta , especially the position reversal and calibration against Start. Existing short-horizon candidates are summarized in Appendix E.2 . The contribution is the controlled characterization of the response in pretrained MeanFlow; the algebraic separation itself is shared with earlier two-time models.

sections.heading: State-grid and query-time calibration.
sections.text: Align Your Steps, Optimal Stepsize Distillation, Optimize Your Sampling, and IntMeanFlow’s O3S change the state/noise grid, with queries tied to state transitions ( Sabour et al., 2024 ; Pei et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Shortcut Models similarly tie the predictor’s step condition to the update span ( Frans et al., 2025 ) . Time-Shift Sampler adjusts a denoiser’s current-time condition ( Li et al., 2024 ) . TimeTuner changes the queried time while retaining the update interval, and MTEO optimizes step- and layer-specific time embeddings while freezing the diffusion backbone ( Xia et al., 2024 ; Cai et al., 2026 ) . Our intervention varies the prediction horizon of an interval-average predictor while fixing its query start and state grid.

sections.heading: Higher-order and adaptive numerical solvers.
sections.text: STORK designs stabilized Runge–Kutta methods for diffusion and flow-matching ODEs ( Tan et al., 2026 ) ; ERK-Guid uses embedded Runge–Kutta local error and stiffness as a guidance signal ( Kong et al., 2026 ) . These methods integrate an instantaneous field, whereas our method changes the queried interval-average prediction. Appendix B.2 points to query-count-matched diagnostics through MeanFlow’s h = 0 h=0 branch; these adapted ports are not native solver implementations.

sections.heading: Guidance along the trajectory.
sections.text: Limited-interval guidance studies the position dependence and accumulated effects of CFG ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) . Our factorial diagnostic holds guidance fixed at and after the intervention, and measures how earlier CFG changes the benefit of a later horizon adjustment. The identified effect concerns the incoming-state distribution.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: Prediction horizon is a separately adjustable inference coordinate in pretrained few-step MeanFlow. Its response is structured: longer horizons hurt near the source and help at the midpoint in our guided CIFAR setting, while earlier guidance changes the midpoint benefit. The useful midpoint effect replicates across training seeds and persists on a stronger frozen state grid. Comparisons with query-start and grid controls show that the preferred choice varies across the tested models, query budgets and evaluators. The evaluated selection procedures use target rollouts. Prediction horizon therefore expands the inference-time design space of few-step MeanFlow with fixed model weights and query count.

sections.heading: Numerical and interpretive scope.
sections.text: Independent audits recompute stored-feature FID and logit-based IS, check selections, query counts, paired stream hashes and source identities. Earlier panels retain stream digests rather than original noise/midpoint tensors; the joint-grid panel additionally saves the canonical metric pixels. Matched real per-image ImageNet features are unavailable, so these studies do not report KID or manifold P/R; the 1008 detector logits are not treated as accuracy against 1000 conditioning labels. Complete candidates, repeat-level cells, numerical provenance and audits remain in the evidence archive. These fixed-model studies establish specific metric orderings under finite budgets, not global optimality or a rule for unseen checkpoints.

sections.text: These are two reused public checkpoints and one historically informed search construction, not independent training replications or search-seed replications. The 2k screening FID uses 2048-dimensional features and can discard useful candidates; this finite comparison establishes neither continuous-family optima nor general dominance. FID and IS do not resolve precision–recall trade-offs. The evidence archive includes every candidate, metric report, seal, audit and runtime scheduling amendment. The portable checker reconstructs selection, contrasts, gates and counts from those reports; it does not re-extract features or recompute image metrics. The original independent audit checked metrics from retained features and artifact hashes without repeating Inception extraction. Image arrays, feature tensors and model weights are outside the portable package.

sections.heading: Appendix D Metric Robustness and Quality–Coverage Trade-offs
sections.text: The seven-checkpoint representation audit and same-pixel Inception reevaluation test whether metric rankings survive a change of evaluator on fixed samples. Both reuse saved samples without new training, generation or schedule search. Correlated metrics are not independent replications.

sections.heading: D.1 Fixed samples and evaluator definitions
sections.text: The main audit uses all seven reused training checkpoints in the 25-candidate CIFAR temporal confirmation, with Local, Start and Horizon fixed at CFG 1.5. Their third queries are ( τ 2 , h 2 ) = ( .5 , .25 ) (\tau_{2},h_{2})=(.5,.25) , ( .575 , .25 ) (.575,.25) and ( .5 , .4895833333 ) (.5,.4895833333) . Each cell retains all 10k images from generation seed 20261502: 210,000 images total. The real reference is the same class-balanced set of 10k CIFAR training images. This is a post-hoc measurement sensitivity study of the 10k calibration panel, distinct from the primary CFG-2 rule and separate 50k endpoint. DINOv2 ViT-S/14 ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) uses 384-dimensional final-LayerNorm CLS features, without L2 normalization, PCA or learned calibration. The frozen official implementation applies PIL bicubic resize to 256, center crop to 224 and ImageNet normalization to real and generated images; its source and weights are hash-bound in the archive. Upsampling and cropping are part of the evaluator. DINO distance is the squared Gaussian Wasserstein distance using float64 empirical moments; manifold precision/recall uses k = 3 k=3 on raw features. These coordinates describe coverage and concentration in the chosen representation, not a single quality score. The original Inception pipeline truncates clipped floating outputs after multiplication by 255. DINO and the original VGG16 fc2_relu P/R pipeline instead consume saved rounded uint8 images. A channel can differ by one uint8 level. To remove that input mismatch, the same-pixel audit passes the saved uint8 tensors directly to the unchanged TorchMetrics/torch-fidelity Inception2015 extractor with normalize=False . The real indices and pixel bytes also match. This produces 2048-dimensional features; FID retains float64 moments and unbiased sample covariance. KID retains the unbiased squared-MMD estimator with a degree-3 polynomial kernel, 100 subsets of 1000 and CPU permutation seed 20261602. No additional rounding or truncation is applied. Inception’s native resizing and DINO’s resize/crop remain different, so the audit compares complete evaluators rather than isolating feature weights. Every checkpoint contributes one paired difference to each descriptive Student- t t interval. All three arm contrasts are reported without multiplicity-adjusted significance claims or outcome-based reselection.

The subset is selected by minimizing mean regret relative to the finite nine-candidate minimum over ( 4 2 ) 2 = 36 \binom{4}{2}^{2}=36 possibilities, separately for NFE 2 and pooled NFE 4/8 contexts; exact ties follow a fixed lexicographic rule. sections.text: The model-defined reference study uses 1,024 states from the historical seed-42 checkpoint. From each state it integrates the next δ = .25 \delta=.25 interval with 16 native local or instantaneous-Heun substeps, obtaining the reference average velocity ( x ref − x ) / δ (x_{\rm ref}-x)/\delta . For each sample it divides the mean squared velocity error by the reference’s mean squared coordinates, with denominator floored at 10 − 12 10^{-12} , then averages over samples. At t = .5 t=.5 , these normalized errors to the native local reference increase with h = .25 , .30 , .375 , .50 h=.25,.30,.375,.50 : .000789/.001268/.003020/.008595. The corresponding instantaneous-Heun errors are .000882/.001370/.003135/.008725. Thus the horizon that improves endpoint FID is not more accurate against these model-defined local references. They are not ground-truth transport paths. The separate analytic two-dimensional diagnostic uses eight Gaussian components on a ring and an analytic conditional-expectation flow field. Two small regressors learn RK4 oracle interval averages, not the MeanFlow objective, and are evaluated after 100, 500 and 2,000 updates: six model–training-stage states, not six independently trained networks. We separate these two quantities at inference, fixing the model, update grid, and number of queries while varying the prediction horizon. Our central finding is that the horizon response depends on both query position and the states entering that query. Across seven independently trained CIFAR-10 checkpoints at classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale 2, a longer horizon worsens FID at early steps but improves it at the midpoint. To probe whether query time alone determines this response, we fix the midpoint query and current/subsequent guidance while changing only earlier CFG. In held-out factorial outcomes on five previously studied checkpoints, the mean midpoint horizon benefit increases from 0.109 to 1.308 FID, indicating sensitivity to the incoming-state distribution. A frozen four-query rule reduces mean CIFAR-10 FID by 2.023 without retraining or extra queries, including gains on five checkpoints trained after rule selection. A milder rule also improves mean FID by 1.041 on a stronger frozen grid, with fixed-rule FID gains on the evaluated public ImageNet-256 and AFHQ checkpoints. However, matched-budget calibration favors query-start shifting in historical CIFAR tests, and the tested Horizon allocation adds no FID benefit beyond Grid+Start on two public ImageNet models. Thus, prediction horizon is a distinct, position- and state-sensitive inference control, but not a universally preferred one. 1 Introduction MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2025 ) predicts an average velocity over an interval and conventionally uses the same interval to advance the state. This couples two decisions: how far the model predicts and how far the sampler moves. Matching them gives the intended displacement for an exact interval-average predictor; a learned predictor’s approximation also depends on the requested interval. Varying prediction horizon independently of update duration exposes an inference choice hidden by their coupling. Let h k h_{k} denote the prediction horizon and δ k = t k + 1 − t k \delta_{k}=t_{k+1}-t_{k} the update duration. We study x k + 1 = x k + δ k ​ u θ ​ ( x k , t k , h k ) , x_{k+1}=x_{k}+\delta_{k}u_{\theta}(x_{k},t_{k},h_{k}), (1) with the model, query start, state grid and query count fixed. Standard inference sets h k = δ k h_{k}=\delta_{k} ; varying only h k h_{k} changes the prediction interval while preserving update duration. Earlier two-time denoisers already separate prediction intervals from output coefficients ( Lee et al., 2026a ; Zilberstein et al., 2026 ) . Our contribution is a controlled characterization of what this choice does in pretrained few-step MeanFlow. Figure 1: Horizon response reverses with position and changes with earlier guidance. Left: seven CIFAR checkpoints at CFG 2, with pointwise 95% Student- t t intervals across checkpoints. Right: five checkpoints with held-out factorial outcomes compare midpoint h 2 = .50 h_{2}=.50 versus .25 .25 after prefix CFG 1 or 1.5; current/later CFG stays 1.5. Lines connect the same checkpoint. Both panels use paired 10k samples per cell, but different guidance settings and checkpoint subsets. The main empirical result is a position-dependent sign reversal in the effect of the queried horizon (Figure 1a). With the checkpoint, state grid, update durations, and guidance fixed, extending a single horizon from 0.25 0.25 to 0.50 0.50 worsens endpoint FID at the source ( t = 0 t=0 ), but improves it at the midpoint ( t = 0.50 t=0.50 ) on all seven independently trained CIFAR checkpoints at CFG 2. A longer prediction horizon is therefore not uniformly beneficial, even at the same extension ratio h / δ = 2 h/\delta=2 . This reversal exposes behavior that cannot be captured by a global horizon multiplier. Crucially, query position alone is insufficient to characterize the horizon response (Figure 1b). We hold the midpoint query time, physical grid, and current/subsequent guidance fixed while changing only CFG in the preceding updates. Within each prefix condition, the two horizon choices share the same incoming states; across prefix conditions, earlier guidance changes the distribution of states reaching the midpoint. In held-out factorial outcomes on five previously studied checkpoints, with the hypothesis frozen before outcome inspection, the mean benefit of midpoint horizon extension increases from 0.109 0.109 to 1.308 1.308 FID. This interaction establishes sensitivity to the incoming-state distribution beyond the query time alone, although it does not isolate the contributions of CFG construction bias, prediction error, or other state-dependent effects. These observations also have practical consequences at fixed inference cost. A frozen four-query horizon rule reduces mean CIFAR-10 FID by 2.023 2.023 across seven checkpoints, including five trained after rule selection. A milder fixed rule retains a mean gain of 1.041 1.041 on a stronger frozen grid, and fixed-rule FID gains extend to the evaluated public ImageNet and AFHQ checkpoints. However, the usefulness of horizon calibration depends on the alternatives: query-start shifts can achieve lower FID/KID, and the tested Horizon allocation provides no additional FID benefit beyond Grid+Start on two public ImageNet models. We therefore distinguish the reproducible response to prediction horizon from whether allocating calibration budget to this control is optimal for a given configuration and evaluator. Our contributions are: • Position-dependent horizon response. We identify a reproducible sign reversal in the effect of extending the queried prediction horizon while preserving the physical state-update grid and model-query count. • Incoming-state dependence. Through a preceding-guidance intervention with the midpoint query and subsequent guidance fixed, we show that the horizon benefit changes with the states entering the query, rather than being determined by query time alone. • Reproducibility and competing controls. We validate frozen horizon rules across training seeds and a stronger state grid, assess fixed-rule transfer to public checkpoints, and compare horizon, query-start, and grid controls under explicit calibration budgets, identifying both benefits and limitations. 2 Prediction Horizon as a Separate Control 2.1 Interval prediction and state evolution Flow Matching learns an instantaneous field v ⁡ ( x , t ) v(x,t) whose ODE transports a source distribution to a data distribution ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) . An exact interval-average predictor favors h = δ h=\delta because the resulting update gives the intended flow displacement. Equation 5 shows what changes for a learned model: varying h h changes both the mismatch between requested and physical intervals and the predictor’s approximation error. The horizon therefore selects how the learned field is queried, in addition to the state grid’s choice of integration steps. The position reversal and incoming-state control reveal structure in this combined response. They leave the relative roles of approximation error and CFG construction bias unresolved; exploratory directional and local-reference studies examine these possibilities in Appendices E.3 and G.3 . The decomposition also clarifies why local prediction accuracy and endpoint performance need separate evaluation. Its two terms are vectors: changing their magnitudes alone does not determine the magnitude of their sum. An endpoint metric additionally evaluates the distribution after the remaining updates, which act on the states produced by the intervention. Agreement with a local reference and improvement of the final distribution therefore answer different questions. In our reference diagnostic, longer midpoint horizons move farther from both the native-local and instantaneous-Heun reference velocities even where endpoint FID improves (Appendix G.3 ). These references are constructed from the learned model, not ground-truth transport trajectories. Their disagreement with FID cautions against using local agreement as a selection criterion on its own; it does not identify the error responsible for the endpoint gain. Selecting the horizon. Once chosen, Horizon adds no velocity queries, but the tested selectors require target rollouts. The preferred temporal control changes across models, NFE values and evaluators, and the tested diagnostic predictor fails its prespecified success criterion (Appendix G.1 ). Practical selection therefore remains target-dependent. More broadly, our experiments separate two questions: whether a model input changes endpoint behavior, and whether allocating calibration budget to that input improves on available alternatives. The position and incoming-state controls establish the former for prediction horizon; the matched-budget comparisons show that the latter is configuration dependent. Scope of the finding. The position reversal and prospective replication are established within one guided CIFAR architecture and training recipe. The blind study adds two training seeds at NFE values already seen in development. Fixed-rule FID gains transfer to the listed public checkpoints, but native iMF interventions fail their benefit criterion (Appendix G.2 ). Together with the Start comparisons and metric trade-offs, this evidence supports configuration-specific horizon calibration. A transferable rule for choosing the horizon remains a separate research challenge. 7 Related Work Few-step MeanFlow inference. The identified effect concerns the incoming-state distribution. 8 Conclusion Prediction horizon is a separately adjustable inference coordinate in pretrained few-step MeanFlow. Its response is structured: longer horizons hurt near the source and help at the midpoint in our guided CIFAR setting, while earlier guidance changes the midpoint benefit. The useful midpoint effect replicates across training seeds and persists on a stronger frozen state grid. Comparisons with query-start and grid controls show that the preferred choice varies across the tested models, query budgets and evaluators. The evaluated selection procedures use target rollouts. Prediction horizon therefore expands the inference-time design space of few-step MeanFlow with fixed model weights and query count.
